editor_note: New shape from today: this is written for me, not for engineers. What AI now costs, how companies are charging for it, where people are already paying, and one for fun. Anything I could not check against a real number was left out.

stories.title: OpenAI cut the price of its cheap model by 80%
stories.summary: OpenAI found ways to run its models more cheaply and has passed the saving on. The cheap tier now costs a fifth of what it did; the middle tier is a fifth cheaper. If you pay for Codex, this also changes how your usage is counted against that subscription, so the saving arrives whether or not you do anything.
stories.fact: From 30 July 2026 GPT-5.6 Luna costs 80% less and Terra 20% less. OpenAI claims Luna matches last year's top models at roughly 6 cents on the dollar per task, at nearly nine times the speed.
stories.take: I pay for Codex, so a Luna price cut lands on my bill without me changing a thing — and it makes leaving agents running overnight a much easier call.
stories.caveat: The six-cents and nine-times figures are OpenAI's own, measured on its own tests. A cheaper model that needs three attempts is not actually cheaper.

stories.title: Why AI prices are falling, and who was making the money
stories.summary: The big labs make most of their profit not from building models but from renting them out afterwards, where the markup is very large. Cheaper open rivals have now got close enough on quality that the markup is getting hard to justify. That is the pressure behind the cuts in the story above.
stories.fact: He puts frontier lab pricing near $25 per million tokens on roughly a 90% gross margin, while the open GLM5.2 runs about $4.40 — under 20% of Opus's retail price.
stories.take: If the margin really is 90%, every price cut I am offered is a fight for my business rather than a favour, and I should keep moving.
stories.caveat: These are one analyst's estimates worked out from public price lists, not audited accounts. Nobody outside the labs knows the true cost of serving a request.

stories.title: Picking your AI on speed, not brains
stories.summary: The top models are now good enough at ordinary work, so the one that answers fastest is often the better buy. He also shows why a much faster model does not make the whole job much faster: waiting on the model is only part of the time, and the rest does not speed up with it.
stories.fact: A task at 50 tokens a second takes 65 seconds start to finish; at 250 it still takes 33. Making the model five times quicker made the actual job only twice as fast.
stories.take: I pick on brains every time, and this says I am paying for cleverness I never actually use on most of my day's tasks.
stories.caveat: He is timing his own working day rather than running a formal test, and a quick answer that is wrong costs more than a slow one that is right.

stories.title: How AI companies charge is changing fast
stories.summary: Charging a flat monthly fee per user is dying out for AI products, because two customers paying the same can cost you wildly different amounts to serve. What is replacing it: a base subscription plus a bill for going over an allowance, the way a phone plan works.
stories.fact: Bessemer, tracking 200+ AI vendors, puts hybrid pricing at 41% in 2026 against 27% in 2025, while per-seat pricing fell from 21% to 15% of SaaS in a year.
stories.take: Everything I sell is priced per user, and a fall from 21% to 15% in a single year says I am pricing on last year's playbook.
stories.caveat: This summarises Bessemer's report rather than being the report, and counting vendors is not counting revenue — plenty of money still sits in per-seat deals.

stories.title: Businesses will pay $10,000 to delete AI's code
stories.summary: A three-person team sells exactly one thing: a week of tearing out the bloat that AI coding tools leave behind. It is a real service at a real price, and it only exists because so many companies now own software nobody on the team understands.
stories.fact: The offer is "One week. Three senior engineers. $10,000", paid in proportion to the result, with one example cutting a codebase from 100,000 lines to 35,000.
stories.take: This is the sharpest demand signal I have seen all week: three engineers making a living cleaning up after the tools I use every single day.
stories.caveat: They publish no client count and no revenue, so it shows people will pay the asking price, not that the market behind it is big.

stories.title: AI budgets are still growing, fast
stories.summary: Company spending on AI is not slowing down. The forecast covers the whole stack — the machines, the software, the services, and the newer tools that do work on their own. For anyone selling to businesses, the budget is sitting there.
stories.fact: Gartner forecasts $2.59 trillion of worldwide AI spending in 2026, up 47% year over year, in a press release dated 19 May 2026.
stories.take: A 47% rise in spending tells me money is not what is stopping my buyers, so when something of mine does not sell, that one is on me.
stories.caveat: A forecast is not a receipt, and this total is mostly hardware and consulting — very different from budget available for a small software product.

stories.title: A benchmark where everyone passes and nobody scores
stories.summary: Someone asks fourteen AI models, three times a month, to draw a frog with a Habsburg jaw. The fun is not really the drawings. It is watching which models cannot resist editorialising about the frog's chin instead of simply drawing what was asked.
stories.fact: All 42 attempts across 14 models produced a valid drawing in August 2026, and the site publishes no score of any kind.
stories.take: I read leaderboards as though they were a score, and 42 out of 42 is a fine reminder that a test everyone passes is measuring nothing.
stories.caveat: Three attempts per model per month, judged purely on taste, so it is a curiosity rather than evidence about any of the models in it.
